June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 
7500 Security Blvd. 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
RE: CMS-0062-P; Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
 
Submitted electronically via regulations.gov. 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
The Kansas Hospital Association appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on CMSâ€™ 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule. The Kansas Hospital 
Association represents 124 acute-care, community hospitals in Kansas, including 83 critical access 
hospitals and 3 rural emergency hospitals.  
 
On behalf of our member hospitals, KHA thanks CMS for its work toward achieving interoperability and 
increasing transparency and beneficiary engagement in prior authorization, as well as efforts to reduce 
administrative burden. We are pleased to see the progress that CMS and commercial insurers have made 
in the last year toward making prior authorization a more patient- and provider-friendly practice and look 
forward to CMS building upon this momentum. 
 
KHA generally supports CMSâ€™ proposed provisions to reduce burdens for rural providers and improve 
patientsâ€™ experiences with the healthcare system. KHA is pleased to see the proposed changes to prior 
authorization, including imposing timeframes for payer decisions on prior authorization requests for 
drugs. More transparency and more detailed information sharing from payers is critical to improve timely 
access to medications and reduce unnecessary administrative burden that payers impose upon hospitals, 
physicians, and clinicians.  
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Requirement To Incorporate Drugs Covered Under a Medical Benefit Into the Prior 
Authorization API for All Impacted Payers 
 
KHA supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service (FFS), Medicaid and CHIP 
managed care plans, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the federal Marketplaces to support 
electronic prior authorization for drugs. This process will help move toward a standardized prior 
authorization process that is easier for patients and providers to navigate and understand.  
 
Proposed Requirement To Support the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard for Prior Authorization for State Medicaid 
and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and 
Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
 
KHA supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to use electronic prior authorization for drugs 
covered under a pharmacy benefit. Combined with the proposal in Section 3 noted above, payers would 
have to support electronic prior authorization for all drugs that require prior authorization. This would 
simplify and streamline prior authorization for physicians and providers, which is often cited as one of the 
 
 
top administrative burdens and in turn delays medically necessary medication and needed care for 
patients. 
 
Proposed Requirement To Support the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard for State Medicaid 
and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and 
Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to adopt the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard 
(RTPB), which MA Part D sponsors are already mandated to adopt by January 1, 2027. NCPDP RTPB 
allows for the real-time exchange of patient data, such as feedback on whether a drug requires prior 
authorization and out-of-pocket costs for the patient. KHA supports the proposal to require impacted 
payers, other than MA organizations, to support the NCPDP RTPB to help expedite patientsâ€™ access to 
prescribed medications. 
 
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorization 
Proposed Requirement To Include a Specific Reason for Denial in Response to Prior Authorization 
Requests for All Drugs 
 
CMSâ€™ proposal to require payers provide a specific reason for denying a prior authorization request is 
another important step toward improved transparency and communication for physicians, providers and 
patients. CMS notes that the specific reason for denying a request should include a specific reason 
that helps the prescribing provider understand why the request was denied and what actions must be 
taken to resubmit or appeal the decision. Examples include information about the specific plan coverage 
criteria on which the denial is based or why documentation did not support the medication or 
prescription. 
 
However, CMS does not provide more guidance on the level of specificity in the proposed regulation 
despite providing examples in the preamble of the proposed rule. KHA urges CMS to adopt 
stronger requirements for a payer to cite a specific reason for an adverse determination in the regulatory 
text. A payer should not be able to use â€œlack of medical necessityâ€ as a reason, which does not provide 
enough information to the prescribing provider and patient to take further action, such as appealing the 
decision or providing more supporting documentation to prove medical necessity. Equipping prescribing 
providers and patients with the most information possible will help to inform a prescribing providerâ€™s 
decision-making process and ensure that action taken is in the best interest of the patient. 
 
KHA suggests that CMS requires payers to provide more specific information on denials, for example, 
indicating what particular part of the beneficiaryâ€™s supporting documentation led the payer to believe 
that the item or service was not medically necessary. Additionally, a broader definition of denial or 
adverse determination should be used. While a course of treatment may be approved, the payer may 
have denied the length of time requested by the provider. This should be included as a denial and the 
payer should explain why, for example, the timeframe for treatment was not approved for the full request 
as prescribed by the physician or other prescribing provider.  
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally Facilitated 
Exchanges 
 
The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule required impacted payers, except 
QHPs on the Federal Marketplaces, to make decisions on prior authorization requests on non-drug 
items and services within 7 days for standard requests and 72 hours for urgent requests. KHA 
supports the proposal to apply this timeframe to QHPs. Aligning regulations for QHPs with other 
 
 
impacted payers will help to minimize administrative burden for prescribing providers as they can expect 
decisions on requests within the same or similar timeframes across patients, regardless of payer. 
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Drugs That Are Not Covered Outpatient Drugs for State 
Medicaid Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, and CHIP Managed Care Entities 
 
KHA supports the proposed alignment of prior authorization timeframe requirements for noncovered 
outpatient drugs with the timeframe for non-drug items and services. That is, Medicaid programs would 
be required to respond to prior authorization requests for non-covered outpatient drugs within 7 calendar 
days for standard requests and 72 hours for urgent requests. Noncovered outpatient drugs may include 
drugs administered in the inpatient setting as part of a bundle of non-drug items and services. CMS 
reasons that these drugs should be subject to the same timeframe as the items and services that they 
are incident to and that the drugs and non-drug items and services are likely submitted together as one 
request. 
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Prescription Drugs for State CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs 
 
CMS proposes to shorten the timeframe for CHIP FFS programs to respond to prior authorization 
requests for drugs for which federal financial participation (FFP) is available. The timeframe would 
reduce to no later than 24 hours after receiving the prior authorization request in order to align with 
existing Medicaid FFS requirements for outpatient drugs. KHA urges CMS to consider applying the 
24-hour timeframe for all payers, including MA organizations and QHPs in future rulemaking. 
 
Proposed Changes to Publicly Reported Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and 
Services for Impacted Payers 
 
In the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, CMS finalized requirements for payers 
to report the percentage of prior authorizations that were approved, denied, approved after appeal, and 
approved after the timeframe for review was extended. CMS proposes to amend these metrics to include 
specific numeric counts. KHA is pleased to see this change as we believe transparency is important for 
payers to report more granular information. Reporting the total number of requests for certain metrics 
will provide a fuller picture of how prior authorization requests are handled and decided upon by payers 
than percentages alone.  
 
KHA supports the proposed new metrics for standard requests: Request denied after timeframe for 
review was extended and request denied after appeal. KHA also supports the new metrics for expedited 
requests: Request approved only after timeframe for review was extended; request approved only after 
appeal; request denied after timeframe for review was extended; and request denied after appeal. 
 
Proposed Requirement To Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics for Drugs for Impacted 
Payers 
 
CMS proposes to add new prior authorization metrics on drugs for impacted payers. These metrics 
largely mirror those used for non-drug items and services and will similarly improve transparency 
in the prior authorization process. 
 
CMS would require impacted payers to report this information on the payersâ€™ public websites. KHA 
suggests that CMS also house this data in one aggregated place on its website so that it is easy for 
enrollees to find and compare across payers. Additionally, patients with lower literacy, including 
technology literacy, will likely not see the benefits of this information posted online even though they 
stand to gain the most from knowing and understanding this information. KHA asks that CMS 
 
 
consider how the prior authorization metrics could be reported to enrollees in other formats, such 
as through opting in to annual mailed reports, so that enrollees may make informed decisions on how 
payers compare. 
 
KHA urges CMS to take action against payers that report a certain percentage of prior 
authorization denials. When a payer reports that over a given percentage, for example, 80%, of all 
requests for a certain item or service are denied, this should trigger an immediate inquiry into the 
payer and its practices. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to offer comments on this proposed rule and for your consideration of our 
comments. We look forward to continuing our work together to ensure our mutual goal of improving 
quality and access to care for patients. Please contact me if you have questions or would like additional 
information. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Karen Braman, RPh, MS 
Senior Vice President, Clinical and Strategic Initiatives
analysis:
# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Kansas Hospital Association (KHA); signed by Karen Braman, RPh, MS, Senior Vice President, Clinical and Strategic Initiatives
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider representative
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents 124 acute-care community hospitals in Kansas, including 83 critical access hospitals and 3 rural emergency hospitals; signatory is a pharmacist and senior clinical/strategic executive.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

KHA generally supports CMS's proposals to expand electronic prior authorization for drugs, align decision timeframes, and increase payer transparency. It urges CMS to strengthen denial-reason specificity, broaden the concept of adverse determinations, centralize public prior authorization metrics, provide non-digital reporting options for enrollees, and investigate payers with unusually high denial rates.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; GENERAL (public prior authorization metrics and transparency)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR sections cited directly; comment references CMS-0062-P and the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule.
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP SCRIPT Standard for Prior Authorization; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB). The comment does not substantively discuss FHIR IGs by name, though it supports the medical-benefit drug Prior Authorization API concept.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic PA for medical benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** KHA says requiring Medicaid/CHIP FFS, Medicaid/CHIP managed care, and QHP issuers on federal Marketplaces to support electronic drug PA would standardize a process that is currently difficult for patients and providers to navigate.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the proposal requiring impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under the medical benefit.

**Topic 2: Electronic PA for pharmacy benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** KHA states that requiring electronic PA for pharmacy-benefit drugs, together with medical-benefit drug PA APIs, would cover all PA-required drugs and reduce provider administrative burden that delays needed medications and care.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the proposal requiring impacted payers to use electronic prior authorization for pharmacy-benefit drugs.

**Topic 3: NCPDP RTPB adoption**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** KHA supports requiring non-MA impacted payers to support NCPDP RTPB because it can provide real-time information on PA requirements and patient out-of-pocket costs.
- **Specific request:** Require impacted payers other than MA organizations to support NCPDP RTPB, aligning with the existing January 1, 2027 MA Part D requirement.

**Topic 4: Specific reasons for drug PA denials**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** KHA supports the proposal but believes the regulatory text is too vague. Generic reasons such as lack of medical necessity do not give providers or patients enough information to appeal, resubmit, or supply missing documentation.
- **Specific request:** Add stronger regulatory-text requirements that denial notices identify the specific coverage criterion or documentation issue, including the particular part of supporting documentation found insufficient.

**Topic 5: Definition of denial/adverse determination**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** KHA notes that a payer may approve treatment but deny the duration or full scope requested, which still affects care and should be transparent.
- **Specific request:** Use a broader definition of denial or adverse determination that includes partial approvals, such as approving treatment for less time than prescribed.

**Topic 6: Drug PA decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** KHA supports aligning QHP timeframes with other impacted payers and aligning non-covered outpatient drug timelines with non-drug items and services. It also supports reducing CHIP FFS prescription-drug PA response time to 24 hours.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the proposed QHP and Medicaid/CHIP timeframe alignments and consider applying a 24-hour drug PA timeframe to all payers, including MA organizations and QHPs, in future rulemaking.

**Topic 7: Public prior authorization metrics**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** KHA supports adding numeric counts and drug-specific PA metrics because percentages alone do not provide a full view of payer behavior. It is concerned that public website posting alone may not reach enrollees with low literacy or technology access.
- **Specific request:** House payer metrics in one CMS-managed location; provide alternate formats such as opt-in mailed annual reports; and trigger CMS inquiry when denial rates exceed a high threshold, such as 80% for a given item or service.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

**Solicitation Responses:**
- **S12:** KHA indirectly supports applying electronic PA to medical-benefit drugs and does not identify specific technical challenges.
- **S14:** KHA supports applying pharmacy-benefit electronic PA requirements to impacted non-Part D payers.
- **S16:** KHA responds directly on what constitutes a specific denial reason, asking CMS to prohibit generic explanations and require actionable detail.
- **S17:** KHA does not request structured denial codes specifically, but its request for more precise denial information is relevant to standardized denial content.
- **S20:** KHA supports a 24-hour CHIP FFS prescription-drug PA timeframe and urges CMS to consider extending that approach to all payers in future rulemaking.
- **S21:** KHA supports the medical-benefit drug electronic PA proposal and does not object to the timeline.
- **S25:** KHA supports NCPDP RTPB adoption and describes real-time information on PA requirements and out-of-pocket costs as beneficial.
- **S43:** KHA supports aligning timeframes across QHPs and Medicaid/CHIP drug categories to reduce provider burden and improve predictability.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic prior authorization requirements for drugs covered under medical benefits.
2. Finalize electronic prior authorization requirements for pharmacy-benefit drugs using NCPDP standards.
3. Require impacted payers other than MA organizations to support NCPDP RTPB.
4. Strengthen regulatory text for denial reasons so payers must provide specific, actionable explanations.
5. Treat partial approvals, such as shortened treatment duration, as denials or adverse determinations requiring explanation.
6. Finalize QHP and Medicaid/CHIP drug PA timeframe alignments.
7. Consider a 24-hour drug PA decision timeframe for all payers in future rulemaking.
8. Require numeric counts in public PA metrics and add drug-specific metrics.
9. Publish prior authorization metrics in a centralized CMS location and offer non-digital reporting options for enrollees.
10. Investigate payers with very high denial rates for particular items or services.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Insufficient specificity in denial notices; continued provider administrative burden; treatment delays; lack of centralized, accessible payer transparency data.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed medically necessary medications and care; inability of providers and patients to understand or appeal denials; inequitable access to online-only public reporting for enrollees with lower literacy or technology literacy.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Not addressed in detail; KHA does not identify major technical implementation barriers.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** KHA represents 124 Kansas acute-care community hospitals, including 83 critical access hospitals and 3 rural emergency hospitals. It gives an illustrative 80% denial-rate threshold for CMS inquiry.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not addressed.
- **Examples provided:** Examples of insufficient denial explanations include generic lack of medical necessity; examples of better explanations include identifying the specific coverage criterion or supporting documentation issue. KHA also provides a partial-approval example where treatment is approved but the requested duration is denied.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Hospitals, physicians, clinicians, prescribing providers, patients, Medicaid/CHIP programs and plans, QHP issuers, MA organizations, and enrollees comparing payer performance.
- **Economic implications:** KHA frames prior authorization as a major administrative burden for providers but does not quantify costs. Streamlined electronic PA and clearer denial explanations could reduce provider rework and appeal burden.
- **Technical feasibility:** KHA expresses support for electronic PA and NCPDP RTPB without raising feasibility objections.
- **Patient care impact:** KHA expects electronic PA, faster timeframes, RTPB information, and more specific denials to improve timely access to medications and reduce delays in medically necessary care.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with targeted modifications
- **Tone:** Professional and collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "KHA generally supports CMS's proposed provisions" - Context: Overall position on the rule.
2. "lack of medical necessity" - Context: Example of an inadequate denial reason.
3. "one aggregated place" - Context: Request for centralized CMS publication of PA metrics.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - KHA repeatedly connects PA standardization, electronic PA, and aligned timeframes to reducing administrative burden on hospitals, physicians, and clinicians.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - KHA notes that enrollees with lower literacy or technology literacy may not benefit from online-only public reporting.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment supports electronic PA and RTPB adoption without raising feasibility objections, indicating confidence in the technical direction.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The central rationale is faster, more predictable access to needed medications and medically necessary care.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - KHA strongly supports more specific denial reasons, numeric PA metrics, drug-specific metrics, centralized publication, and denial-rate oversight.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment emphasizes simplifying and standardizing PA processes across payers so providers can work within more predictable workflows.
